title: Special memories
summary: Not every memory is a plain single-port SRAM. Memories with **ECC**, **multi-port** memories and memories in other **clock domains** each change what MBIST must do.
objectives: Explain why MBIST bypasses ECC and how the ECC logic itself is tested.
Describe what extra testing multi-port memories need.
Explain how MBIST handles clock domains and runs at speed.

blocks.md: Many memories store extra **check bits** and use an **error-correcting code** (ECC): an encoder computes the check bits on every write, a decoder corrects a flipped bit on every read. How ECC works is covered in the memory courses of *Digital Design*; here we only ask how to **test** such a memory.

steps.title: ECC hides faults
steps.md: If MBIST tested through the ECC, a stuck-at cell would simply be **corrected** — the test would pass. The chip would ship with a defect, and with no margin left for a second error in the field.

steps.title: Test the array with ECC bypassed
steps.md: MBIST writes and reads the **full code word** — data bits and check bits — directly. Every cell, including the check bits, gets the March test.

steps.title: Test the ECC logic
steps.md: Then the encoder and decoder are checked: write a code word with **one flipped bit** (or two) through the bypass, read it through the decoder, and check the corrected data and the **error flags**.

blocks.title: ECC in the field
blocks.md: During operation ECC corrects soft errors, and error counters tell the system when a memory is getting worse. How ECC, scrubbing and periodic MBIST work together is a topic of *BIST in the Field*.

items.title: Test every port
items.md: Each port has its own address decoder, read and write circuits. The March test is run **through each port**, so a faulty decoder of port B is not hidden by a good port A.

items.title: Port-interaction faults
items.md: Two ports working at the same time share bit lines and cells. Faults may appear only when port A **reads** while port B **writes** the same row or column. **Two-port March tests** run operations on both ports in the same clock.

items.title: Register files
items.md: Small, many ports, very fast. They are tested like multi-port memories; very small ones built from flip-flops may be tested by **scan** instead of MBIST.

blocks.caption: Configuration and results cross between the slow and the fast clock through synchronizers

items.title: The controller lives in the memory's clock domain
items.md: To test at speed, the controller and the collar run on the **same clock as the memory**. Memories in different clock domains get **different controllers**.

items.title: Crossing from TAP to the controller
items.md: Configuration and results travel through the slow JTAG clock (TCK). Signals such as *start* and *done* cross between TCK and the memory clock through **synchronizers**.

items.title: Where the fast clock comes from
items.md: On the tester, the chip's own **PLL** usually provides the at-speed clock; the tester only supplies a slow reference. MBIST is often repeated at several **voltages** and **temperatures** to find weak cells.

questions.text: Why must MBIST bypass the ECC when it tests the memory cells?
options: Otherwise single faulty cells are corrected and the test would pass.
ECC makes the memory too slow for MBIST.
ECC changes the addresses.
MBIST cannot write check bits.

questions.text: The check-bit cells must be tested by MBIST as well as the data cells.
options: True
False

questions.text: How is the ECC decoder tested?
options: Store a code word with flipped bits through the bypass and read it through the decoder.
Run March C− through the decoder.
Measure the decoder's power.
It does not need a test.

questions.text: Why is a March test run through **each** port of a dual-port memory?
options: Each port has its own decoder and read/write circuits that can be faulty.
The memory content is different on each port.
One port is only for ECC.
To make the test twice as fast.

questions.text: Two memories run on different functional clocks. What does MBIST usually do?
options: Use a separate controller for each clock domain
Test both on the JTAG clock
Test only the faster one
Merge the two clocks

questions.text: Which signals cross between the JTAG clock and the memory clock?
options: Control and status such as start and done
Every memory address
Every read data word
None — both run on TCK
